title: Stocks, outages and the crack: OLS, residuals, White's test and HC3 standard errors
concepts: what robust SEs do not fix

explain.prompt: The trader asks: “So is the widening physical? And can I trust the numbers?” Answer in 5–7 sentences: interpret the stocks and outage coefficients in their units, say what the White test rejects and what HC3 changes — and what it does not change — and name one way the model is still wrong.
rubric: Stocks coefficient: −1.09 $/bbl of monthly gasoil crack per percentage point of stocks below their 5-year average — a 20 % deficit, as in 2022, is worth about +22 $/bbl. Strongly significant with either standard error.
Outages: +2.8 $/bbl per 1,000 kb/d offline; p = 0.046 with conventional SEs but 0.21 with HC3 — the evidence rests on a few large-outage months and does not survive robust inference.

White's LM statistic is 26.6 (p = 0.002): we reject constant error variance. The residual standard deviation is 4.95 $/bbl when stocks are more than 15 % below average against 1.67 near average — a tight market is a volatile market.
HC3 changes the standard errors (× 1.5 for stocks, × 1.6 for outages), hence t-statistics, p-values and intervals. It does not change the coefficients, the fitted values, the residuals or R² (0.93).

HC3 does not fix a misspecified model: residuals average +0.99 when stocks are below −15 % and −1.42 between −15 % and −5 % — the crack responds convexly to scarcity and a straight line misses it. Durbin-Watson 1.36 also signals autocorrelated residuals, which HC3 ignores.

Conclusion: the widening is consistent with a physical stock deficit (a robust coefficient), the outage effect is not robustly established, and the model's form — not just its standard errors — needs work before it is used for sizing. VIFs of 1.0–1.2 rule out multicollinearity as the explanation.
